sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A warm front has introduced a very mild air mass to Western Washington with near record high temperatures expected today. A cold front will stall offshore into Thursday with mainly dry conditions for interior areas and light rain at times near the coast. A series of frontal systems will bring a return of widespread rain and occasionally windy conditions Friday into early next week.

sections.title: Short term (today through Friday)
paragraphs: Rain has ended for most areas except for a few showers near the coast early this morning. Temperatures are extraordinarily mild across the region in the wake of a warm front that lifted north across Western Washington late yesterday. Windy conditions will continue along the coast and across the north interior, but are expected to ease late today. A cold front will stall offshore today into Thursday. Areas of light rain will occasionally skirt the coast and Olympic Peninsula ahead of this boundary, but the remainder of the area is expected to be largely dry with high temperatures, especially today, threatening some daily records.

A fairly deep upper trough moving across the Gulf of Alaska will push an occluded front onshore into the region during the day on Friday. Fortunately, this system looks like it will be vertically stacked upon arrival...thereby losing a lot of its punch before coming ashore. Nonetheless, it will bring another round of rain along with breezy to locally windy conditions. It will also churn up some pretty large surf during its offshore journey with seas of 20+ feet reaching coastal areas again by Friday night.

sections.title: Long term (Friday night through Tuesday)
paragraphs: A trailing upper trough is expected to quickly swing onshore Friday night. Another potent front approaches the region on Saturday night. Though this system is also vertically stacked, the path of the surface low gives it better wind potential, especially for the coast, along with a fairly deep moisture feed. And, as such, WPC has placed a large swath of the Olympic Peninsula under marginal risk in their Excessive Rainfall Outlook for 12Z Saturday to 12Z Sunday. Plenty of post-frontal showers are expected to spread onshore into Sunday keeping things fairly soggy. There's still decent model agreement with a brief break for Monday, but the key word is brief. Another wet and potentially windy front arrives in the Tuesday time frame. It might have started slow, but November as we know it is well and truly here now.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Southwest flow aloft continues into tonight with a stalled frontal boundary over the offshore waters. Areas of MVFR in light rain will continue through the morning for coastal areas while VFR is expected for the interior under varying amounts of mid and high level cloud cover. Gusty southerly surface winds along the coast and across the north interior are expected to ease later today. With lighter surface winds expected tonight, there is an increased risk of areas of IFR low clouds forming west of Puget Sound, across the Southwest Interior, and far south Puget Sound on Thursday morning.
KSEA...VFR with varying amounts of high and mid level clouds today. Surface winds south to southeasterly 7 to 10 knots easing to 6 knots or less tonight.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Strong winds will continue to persist across the coastal waters through much of the day today as a cold front remains stalled offshore. This front will weaken as it slowly drifts onshore this evening, allowing winds to slowly ease this evening into early Thursday morning. Gale Warnings for the coastal waters and East Strait of Juan de Fuca, and Northern Inland Waters, and Small Craft Advisories for Admiralty Inlet will continue through evening as well. Seas 13 to 15 ft this morning may creep slightly upward towards 16 to 18 ft, but generally remaining in the 14 to 16 ft range through tonight. Seas will ease to around 11 to 13 ft on Thursday.

A pair of strong low pressure systems will move across the coastal waters late Thursday night into Friday, with the second moving through Saturday night into Sunday. Winds will begin to increase across the area waters on Thursday. Gales will begin as early as Thursday afternoon, through winds look to peak overnight into early Friday morning. Guidance continues to indicate 50-70% chances for storm force gusts over the outer coastal waters, but confidence has decreased for the inner coastal waters with high-end gales the more likely scenario there. Winds will ease Friday night before increasing again Saturday with a secondary peak Saturday evening. Gale force winds again are very likely across the coastal waters, with 40-50% chances for storm force gusts over the outer coastal waters.

Seas once again will build over the coastal waters on Friday. With the low center tracking closer towards our area, that will send the largest waves farther south towards Oregon. That being said, very large seas are expected, with ensemble guidance continuing to show very high confidence (>90%) in seas above 20 ft by Friday evening, with a 25-35% chance of seas above 25 ft through Saturday morning. Dominant periods will be very long, in the 16-18 s range. Seas look to briefly ease Saturday morning below 20 ft before another system will send another round of large, long period waves on Sunday with high (70-80%) confidence in seas above 20 ft with a 15-30% chance of seas exceeding 25 ft through early Monday.

With these systems, slight shifts in the low tracks will determine where the strongest wave generation/dynamic fetch regions will be. While it is looking more likely that the largest waves will be aimed towards Oregon and California from the Friday/Saturday system, the Sunday/Monday system favors a more northward track with the largest waves aimed towards the Washington coast. There is a 5-10% chance of waves exceeding 30 ft at the peak wave height Sunday night.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: Drier weather Wednesday and Thursday will give way to another series of storm systems beginning Friday and continuing into next week. Sneaker waves will be a threat through the week with another round of high surf conditions appearing increasingly likely Friday night into Saturday.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Drier weather Wednesday and Thursday will give way to another series of storm systems beginning Friday and continuing into next week. Sneaker waves will be a threat through the week with another round of high surf conditions appearing increasingly likely Friday night into Saturday.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Monday...Radar imagery and surface observations as of early Tuesday afternoon depicts a band of rain over far northwest Oregon and southwest Washington as an atmospheric river pushes into the Pacific Northwest and British Columbia. Moisture that is being squeezed between upper-level troughing over the Gulf of Alaska and upper-level ridging over the Great Basin and southwestern U.S. has become an atmospheric river aimed towards our area. High pressure to our south is resulting in a pretty distinct line between rain and dry conditions. Most of the rain over the past 12 hours has been north of a line from Newport, OR to The Dalles, OR. Surface observations have shown rain amounts between 0-0.10" for locations along this line and southward, while areas to the north have received anywhere from 0.25 to 1 inch in the last 12 hours. The heaviest rain amounts have been further north over the Olympic Peninsula. Breezy southerly winds continue along the coast through this afternoon with gusts to 30-40 mph. Inland, winds are generally coming out of the southeast but remaining under 10 mph. Tonight, upper-level ridging will build over the area, gradually decreasing rain and returning drier conditions.

Upper-level ridging will reach its peak amplitude on Wednesday, supporting dry and unseasonably warm temperatures across interior valleys with high temperatures forecast in the mid to upper 60s. Daily record high temperatures could be broken tomorrow, including the 64F record at Portland (PDX) and Hillsboro (HIO) set in 1989, and 66F at Vancouver (VUO) set in 1904, 1907, and 1930 may be in jeopardy. However, a 20-40% chance for showers will continue in Pacific County and along the coast north of Tillamook. Thursday is also looking to be a mostly dry day with similar chances for showers along the north Oregon and south Washington coast. Daytime temperatures will lower a few degrees, though will still be unseasonably warm in the low 60s across interior valleys. By Thursday night, upper- level ridging will begin to shift eastward as upper-level troughing begins pushing into the northeast Pacific.

There is high confidence that a deep upper-level trough will become situated over the northeast Pacific west of Canada from late Thursday/Friday into the weekend, returning troughing to the Pacific Northwest. Multiple surface frontal systems are expected to move through the region during this time, bringing repeated chances for widespread rain and breezy winds. There is still uncertainty with specific rainfall amounts and peak wind gusts; however, we can say for certain that it will be wet. This is shaping up to be another atmospheric river event as long- range ensembles indicate a 60-70% chance for vapor transport to exceed 500 kg/(ms) at the leading edge of this trough on Friday somewhere along the Oregon coast with similar probabilities of vapor transport values remaining above 250 kg/(ms) into Sunday. Increasingly saturated soils from multiple weather systems could allow for greater runoff into area rivers, meaning at least isolated flooding cannot be ruled out. However, chances for widespread flooding of rivers remains <5% at this time. It's still too far out to determine hourly rainfall rates, but if rain is heavy enough, we could also see some urban and small stream flooding of low-lying and poor drainage areas. People should make sure to clear gutters and storm drains of any leaves or debris.

Across the Cascades, it appears that this system will be warm enough to keep snow levels between 5500-6500 feet on Friday, keeping the passes snow-free. By Saturday, snow levels drop to around 5000 ft, potentially bringing some light snow to Willamette Pass. From Friday afternoon to Sunday afternoon, there is a 30% chance for total snowfall amounts of 1 inch or greater along Santiam and Willamette Passes, and a 10% chance along Highway 26 at Government Camp. Much higher snowfall amounts expected above 6000-6500 feet.

When it comes to winds, there is a 20-40% chance for maximum wind gusts exceeding 55 mph along the coast Friday and Saturday, with the highest chances on Friday. Wind gusts of this magnitude could result in scattered or widespread power outages or tree damage. Along the I-5 corridor, there is a 5-15% chance for maximum wind gusts exceeding 40 mph, which could result in isolated power outages or tree damage. To prepare, make sure to secure loose outdoor items.
Heading into early next week, the vast majority of ensemble members show some degree of troughing over the West Coast, maintaining a generally cool and wet pattern.     -10/03

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 06Z Thursday...A warm front shifted northward into Washington earlier today. This led to most low clouds shifting north of the region. High clouds should continue to stream across the region, but remain thin enough that the surface will gradually decouple with patches of fog and low clouds developing in wind sheltered locations. Despite only 10-20% of the high resolution ensembles suggesting fog development in the Willamette Valley overnight, have opted to include it in the TAFs for KEUG, KSLE, KUAO and KHIO for now with several of these sites having already dipping into LIFR thresholds. Western Willamette Valley sites will be more prone to IFR conditions sticking around longer into the day on Wednesday as low level easterly to southeasterly flow upslope into the Coast Range. Meanwhile, gusty southerly winds along the coast will continue through the taf period with gusts generally hovering between 15-25 kt. Similarly, expect easterly wind gusts of around 15- 25 kt at KTTD.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...A warm front has lifted north of the region with thinning cloud cover over the terminal. Easterly winds continue at the surface, which should help to keep conditions VFR overnight into Wednesday. If winds temporarily weaken, fog and/or low clouds will develop or move upriver into the terminal quickly overnight, but at this point, the probability of that scenario appears less than 20%.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A frontal boundary draped across the waters is supporting hazardous conditions to some degree for all zones. Currently, a Gale Warning is in effect for waters north of Cape Falcon, including the Columbia River Bar while Hazardous Seas Warnings are in place south of Cape Falcon to Florence. The Gale Warning expands southward to zones PZZ272 and PZZ252 later this evening. Wind gusts around 40 kt are expected through Wednesday afternoon before headlines transition to Hazardous Seas Warnings for all zones. A building west swell will increase seas to 14-17 ft around 14 seconds through Wednesday. Hazardous Seas conditions are expected to continue through Wednesday night before possibly dropping down to Small Craft Advisory conditions.

A brief lull in activity is expected on Thursday before ramping back up late Thursday evening. Another strong front is expected to move into the waters, likely bringing at least Gales with a 70-80% chance and a 10-30% chance for Storms (highest in the outer waters). Seas are again expected to rise above 20 ft by Friday afternoon with a 30-50% chance for greater than 25 ft and a 10-15% chance for 30 ft or greater in the outer waters. Another strong front is expected during the latter half of Saturday, continuing the active pattern for the waters.   -19

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: A moderate to high sneaker wave threat continues along the coast through this week as a westerly swell of 10-12 ft at 13-15 seconds increases to 14-16 ft midweek. This will result in waves running up significantly farther on a beach than normal, including over rocks and jetties. Sneaker waves can suddenly knock people off of their feet and quickly pull them into the frigid ocean which may lead to serious injury or drowning.
There is also the potential for tidal overflow flooding Wednesday as the tide plus anomaly are forecasted between 10 and 11 ft (MLLW). This could lead to further water inundation and coastal erosion.

Additionally, confidence is increasing that a stronger westerly swell of 18-22 ft with a dominant period at 16-18 seconds will impact the coast on Saturday for dangerous surf conditions. Destructive waves may wash over beaches, jetties, and other structures unexpectedly.

Extreme caution should be used if you plan to visit beaches this week. The large wave runup may dislodge logs on area beaches and result in them rolling up and down area beaches, which have historically killed or seriously injured unsuspecting people, so there will be much more of a threat than just getting wet from a rogue wave.
